directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean soil after the last frost, spacing plants to allow the trailing stems room to knit together into a dense carpet. Imperial Purple produces small clustered flowers in a richer, darker violet-purple than typical seed-grown trailing lantana, held above gray-green aromatic foliage through the warm months. It is extremely heat and drought tolerant once rooted in, making it a reliable choice for slopes, retaining walls, and hanging baskets where water is limited. In zone 8 it usually dies back to the crown after hard freezes and regrows readily from the roots in spring.

Grow in full sun in sharply drained, low-fertility soil, ideally with a limestone or sandy base that mimics its native Miami pine rockland habitat. Pineland lantana is a low, sprawling subshrub bearing small flower heads that open yellow and age to orange, giving a two-toned effect on the same cluster. It is extremely drought tolerant once established and should never be planted near Lantana camara, since the two readily hybridize and threaten the genetic integrity of this rare native. Occasional light pruning keeps growth dense and encourages continuous bloom for native bees and small butterflies.
sources: Institute for Regional Conservation — Floristic Inventory of South Florida

directions: Plant in a lightly shaded to partly sunny spot with consistently moist, well-drained soil, as this species tolerates more shade and moisture than the typical sun-loving garden lantanas. Dense, upright spikes of small lilac to pink-purple flowers appear year-round in frost-free areas, followed by clusters of glossy purple-black berries that birds readily eat. It naturalizes along hammock edges and disturbed tropical woodland margins throughout its Caribbean and Central American range, and performs well as an informal understory shrub in South Florida landscapes. Prune lightly after flowering flushes to maintain a tidy, multi-stemmed form.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

directions: Grow in full sun in thin, alkaline, fast-draining soil that mirrors the limestone outcrops and coastal berms of its native Florida Keys and Bahamian range. Rounded clusters of small white to pale cream flowers with a faint yellow throat appear through the warm months, drawing skippers and small butterflies, and are followed by dark berries favored by songbirds. It tolerates salt spray and brief drought well once established, making it a dependable choice for seaside native gardens where many other flowering shrubs struggle. Trim lightly after bloom flushes to keep the naturally compact, rounded habit tidy.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)
Institute for Regional Conservation — Floristic Inventory of South Florida

directions: Hagenia abyssinica is the sole species in its genus, a fast-growing, dioecious tree of the Afromontane forest belt across Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania, typically found between 2,500 and 3,400 meters elevation. Its large, fern-like pinnate leaves and showy drooping panicles of reddish flowers, historically used as the anthelmintic 'kosso,' make it a striking specimen for highland gardens and arboreta in frost-free to lightly frosty climates. Grow young transplants in full sun on well-drained, fertile soil with reliable moisture, siting it where summers stay cool and winters remain mild. Because it grows quickly from seed, it also features in East African reforestation and agroforestry plantings as well as specialty collections of cool-growing tropical highland trees.
sources: Kew Gardens Plants of the World Online

directions: Juniperus procera is the dominant conifer of the East African highland forest belt, forming extensive stands on Mount Kenya, the Ethiopian highlands, and other Afromontane ranges between roughly 1,500 and 3,000 meters. It develops into a tall, often single-trunked tree with reddish, fibrous bark and juvenile scale foliage that matures to typical juniper sprays, long valued for durable, aromatic timber known as East African 'cedar.' Plant transplants in full sun on well-drained soil in a climate with cool highland-style summers and mild winters. Established trees are drought-tolerant once rooted and are occasionally grown outside Africa in mild-winter collections of African conifers.
sources: Kew Gardens Plants of the World Online

directions: The Ethiopian giant lobelia is an iconic rosette-forming species of the afro-alpine moorland of the Bale and Simien Mountains, spending years as a tight rosette of long, strap-shaped leaves before sending up a single towering flowering spike densely packed with small greenish-purple blooms. Grow it in a cool, humid site with sharply draining but moisture-retentive soil, mimicking the strong diurnal frost-to-warmth swings of its native afro-alpine zone. It is monocarpic, flowering only once after many years of rosette growth before setting seed and dying, so collectors typically keep plants of staggered ages. Specialist alpine and succulent growers occasionally raise it from seed obtained through rare-seed suppliers, succeeding outdoors only in a handful of exceptionally mild, humid gardens.
sources: Kew Gardens Plants of the World Online

directions: Dendrosenecio keniodendron, the Mount Kenya giant groundsel, is one of the most distinctive plants of the East African afro-alpine zone, forming a slow-growing, tree-like rosette shrub with a thick insulating skirt of dead leaves wrapped around the stem to buffer nightly freezes at its native elevation above 3,500 meters. In cultivation it needs a cool, humid, frost-adapted environment with sharp drainage and shelter from prolonged hot, dry weather, conditions difficult to replicate outside specialist alpine houses or exceptionally mild, oceanic gardens. It grows extremely slowly, taking many years to branch and flower, and is grown mainly by botanic gardens and dedicated collectors of African high-mountain flora. A small number of specialist seed suppliers offer seed collected from cultivated stock.

Erythrina abyssinica, the red-hot-poker tree, is a small to medium deciduous tree of East African highland grassland and forest-margin habitats, recognized by its corky, deeply fissured bark and dense, upright spikes of bright red-orange flowers that appear on bare branches before the leaves emerge. It is widely planted as an ornamental and shade tree across its native range and is occasionally grown in frost-free to nearly frost-free gardens elsewhere for its striking winter floral display. Grow from scarified seed or transplants in full sun on well-drained soil, and expect flowering within a few years of establishment. It tolerates poor, rocky soils and seasonal drought well but is sensitive to frost and prolonged wet conditions.
sources: Kew Gardens Plants of the World Online

directions: Dovyalis abyssinica, known locally in Ethiopia as koshim, is a thorny, highland-adapted fruiting shrub closely related to the better-known kei-apple, bearing small, tart, orange-yellow fruits used traditionally for preserves and fresh eating. It grows naturally along Afromontane forest margins and highland thickets across Ethiopia and neighboring East African highlands, tolerating cooler nights and higher elevations better than most tropical Dovyalis species. Plant transplants in full sun on well-drained soil, and prune to control its vigorous, spiny growth and keep fruit within reach. It is grown mainly by tropical and subtropical fruit specialists and home orchardists seeking unusual, cold-hardier relatives of more familiar African gooseberry-type fruits.

The prickly blue poppy is a true alpine scree specialist from the high Himalaya and adjacent Tibetan Plateau, typically found above 4,000 meters on open stony slopes, and is immediately recognizable by the dense covering of bristly, blue-based spines on its leaves and flower stems. Its clear, pale to deep blue flowers are carried singly or in small clusters on short stems rising directly from a basal rosette, opening in summer against bare scree. Because it is monocarpic and demands cool summers with sharp drainage, it is usually grown from seed in alpine-house pots plunged in sand or grit, or in a raised scree bed. It is a benchmark challenge plant among dedicated alpine gardeners.

The lampshade poppy takes its name from its large, nodding, clear yellow flowers with overlapping petals that form a shallow bowl above a rosette of soft, hairy leaves, growing naturally in open alpine meadows and scrub across the eastern Himalaya and adjoining Chinese mountains. Like its blue-flowered relatives, it prefers cool, humid summers and consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil, performing best in maritime mountain climates such as the Pacific Northwest or the Scottish Highlands. It is typically monocarpic or short-lived, flowering spectacularly in its second or third year before setting seed and declining, so growers often raise a fresh batch of seedlings every year or two. Specialist seed exchanges and alpine nurseries are the main source.

Androsace muscoidea is a tiny, densely cushion-forming rock jasmine from high rocky and gravelly Himalayan slopes, where its tightly packed rosettes of small, hairy leaves form a moss-like mat only an inch or two tall. In late spring it covers itself with small white to pale pink flowers with a yellow eye, held just above the cushion on short stalks. It demands the sharp drainage and lean, gritty soil typical of true scree and trough alpines, and resents winter wet far more than cold, so growers top-dress the crown with grit and often provide an overhead rain shelter in wet climates. It is grown almost exclusively by dedicated alpine and rock garden specialists.

Primula reptans is one of the smallest and most prostrate of the Himalayan primulas, forming a creeping mat of tiny, farinose rosettes that hug gravel and rock crevices on high alpine scree slopes across Nepal, Sikkim, and Tibet. Its small, clear lavender to lilac flowers with a yellow eye are carried almost at ground level in late spring, nestled directly among the foliage. In cultivation it requires the same sharp drainage, gritty scree mix, and cool summer conditions favored by other high-alpine primulas. It remains a true specialist's plant, propagated and traded mainly through alpine garden society plant sales and seed exchanges.

Gentiana ornata is a diminutive, mat-forming gentian native to high alpine scree and turf of the Himalaya, from Nepal through Sikkim and Bhutan, hugging the ground among rock fragments at elevations above 4,000 meters. Its relatively large, upward-facing deep blue flowers, often with greenish spotting in the throat, open in late summer and autumn directly above a low cushion of narrow leaves. It wants the same sharp, mineral drainage and cool root run favored by other true scree gentians, planted in a gritty raised bed or trough. Specialist alpine nurseries and rock garden society seed exchanges are the principal sources.

Musk larkspur is named for the distinctive musky fragrance of its foliage, a trait unusual among delphiniums, and it grows naturally on open, stony alpine slopes and scree across the Himalaya from Kashmir to Tibet at elevations up to 5,000 meters. Short, sturdy stems carry a few relatively large, hooded, blue-purple flowers above a low tuft of rounded, lobed leaves, blooming in mid to late summer. Grow it in full sun in a sharply drained, gritty scree mix, allowing winter dormancy with minimal wet around the crown. It remains an uncommon plant outside specialist alpine garden circles.

Cassiope fastigiata is a Himalayan counterpart to the circumpolar arctic heathers, forming dense, wiry evergreen mats or hummocks of tiny, closely overlapping scale-like leaves on slender stems across high-elevation moorland and rocky ground from Nepal to southwestern China. Small, nodding, white bell-shaped flowers appear on fine red stalks in late spring, held just above the foliage much as in its arctic relatives. It needs cool, humid summers, acidic, humus-rich, consistently moist but well-drained soil, and reliable winter snow cover, making it suited to cool temperate rock gardens and peat beds. It is propagated mainly by cuttings or careful division and traded chiefly through specialist ericaceous and alpine plant nurseries.

Rhodiola crenulata, known in traditional Tibetan and Chinese medicine as hong jing tian, is a succulent-leaved perennial of high alpine rock and scree habitats across the Himalaya and Tibetan Plateau, typically found above 3,500 meters. Its thick, fleshy rootstock and gray-green, toothed leaves support clusters of small reddish to yellow-green flowers in late spring, and the root has become a commercially significant adaptogenic herb in the global herbal supplement trade. Grow it in full sun in gritty, well-drained, lean soil, since it is highly cold-hardy but prone to rot in humid, poorly drained, or hot-summer conditions. It is available both as a living garden plant from specialty medicinal-herb and alpine nurseries and as dried root material in the herbal trade.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

directions: This fine-textured Commelinaceae relative of wandering jew forms a low, spreading mat of slender green leaves topped with tiny three-petaled white flowers held just above the foliage. It thrives as a living groundcover beneath tree canopies or large-leaved tropicals in zone 9-11 shade beds, knitting together quickly once established. Keep soil evenly moist and shear back lightly in spring to refresh dense new growth. It also works well tumbling over the edges of shaded raised beds or container plantings.

This Mexican and Central American understory shrub earns its common name from quilted, puckered leaves that shimmer with a satiny sheen in dappled light and reveal wine-purple undersides when the foliage moves. It is grown strictly as a foliage accent in deeply shaded tropical beds, where its texture contrasts beautifully against broader-leaved companions. Protect it from wind and direct sun, which quickly scorch the delicate leaf surface, and keep the root zone consistently humid. Light feeding during the warm season keeps new growth colorful.

A variegated sport of the Pacific lettuce tree, this large soft-wooded shrub carries broad, crinkled leaves splashed cream and pale green in horizontal tiers, giving it a striking layered silhouette in shaded tropical landscapes. Filtered light or morning sun with afternoon shade keeps the variegation crisp without scorching, while deep shade tends to mute the pattern back toward green. It is commonly used as an understory specimen or informal screen in zone 10-11 gardens and tolerates occasional pruning to control its size. Give it rich, well-drained soil and steady moisture during active growth.

Native to understory forest from the Himalayan foothills through Southeast Asia, this bold aralia relative produces huge, deeply lobed leaves with a felted, snowflake-like outline that make it a dramatic focal point in shaded tropical beds. New growth emerges wrapped in fuzzy, spine-tipped stipules before unfurling into the mature leaf shape. It performs best in bright, filtered shade with shelter from strong wind, which can tatter the broad leaves. In frost-prone parts of its range it is often grown in large containers and moved under cover for winter.

This Philippine aralia forms a tidy, upright shrub of narrow, deeply cut green leaves that give it a fine, almost parsley-like texture quite different from its broad-leaved relatives. It is widely planted as a low hedge or foundation grouping in frost-free gardens, tolerating both filtered shade and partial sun once established. Regular light trimming keeps the naturally dense habit tight, and it recovers quickly from pruning. Even moisture and a mulched root zone help it hold its color through the warm season.

Sarilop is the original Aegean fig cultivar, long grown around Aydin and Izmir in western Turkey, from which cuttings sent to California in the 1880s became the famous Calimyrna fig. As a true Smyrna type it depends on pollination by the tiny fig wasp carrying pollen from an inedible caprifig, without which the main late-summer crop drops before ripening. The ripe fruit has thin golden-green skin and dense amber flesh with a rich, nutty sweetness, traditionally dried whole on open-air mats to produce the pale, chewy dried figs long exported from the region. Grow it in deep, well-drained soil with minimal winter pruning and steady moisture while fruit sizes up to reduce splitting.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Fig Fruit Facts
UC Davis Fruit & Nut Research & Information Center — Fig Cultivars

directions: Sigoise takes its name from the town of Sig in the olive-growing plains of western Algeria, where it has long been grown as the country's leading table olive rather than as an oil cultivar. Its fruit is notably large and elongated compared with most Mediterranean olives, with a thick flesh-to-pit ratio well suited to brine-curing for both green and ripe black table olives. Plant grafted trees in full sun on well-drained soil with a compatible pollinator cultivar nearby, since olives bear more reliably with cross-pollination. Harvest green for classic cracked or brined olives, or let fruit darken on the tree for a milder, oil-richer black-cured product.
sources: International Olive Council — World Catalogue of Olive Varieties
Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations — olive germplasm records, Algeria

common_name: Kavilca Wheat (Black Sea Anatolian Hulled Wheat Landrace)
directions: Kavilca is an ancient hulled wheat landrace, related to emmer, that has survived on small highland plots of Turkey's Western Black Sea region long after most farmers switched to free-threshing bread and durum wheats. Its tough hull clings to the kernel even after threshing, requiring an extra dehulling step before milling, but the payoff is a dense, nutty-flavored flour now being revived by a small wave of artisan bakeries and specialty mills. Sow in autumn into tilled upland ground and rely on winter and spring rainfall rather than irrigation. Traditional uses include a coarse bulgur and a dense, chewy flatbread with a flavor distinct from products made from modern bread wheat.
sources: Morgounov et al., 'Wheat Landraces Currently Grown in Turkey', Crop Science, 2016
Republic of Turkey Bahri Dagdas International Agricultural Research Institute — Wheat Landraces Inventory of Turkey

directions: Ardhaoui is a traditional six-row barley landrace grown across the drier central and southern reaches of Tunisia, where generations of rainfed cultivation on thin, marginal soils selected it for drought and heat tolerance rather than yield. Its grain has long been roasted and ground for bsissa, a barley-and-legume flour mixed with olive oil, dates, or honey, as well as for coarse traditional breads eaten throughout rural Tunisia. Sow into tilled ground in autumn so the crop establishes on early-winter rainfall and finishes its cycle before the dry heat of early summer. Because of its resilience and genetic diversity, Ardhaoui accessions remain an active focus of Tunisian and regional barley conservation and breeding programs.
sources: International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) — Barley Genetic Resources, North Africa
Institut National de la Recherche Agronomique de Tunisie (INRAT) — Tunisian barley landrace characterization

directions: Mahmoudi is an old durum wheat landrace from the semi-arid grain belts of central and northern Tunisia, long valued by smallholders for its hard, glassy amber kernels that mill into the coarse semolina used for hand-rolled couscous and local breads. Like other Tunisian durum landraces maintained in national genebank collections, it has persisted for generations on rainfed ground where deep rooting and tolerance of erratic winter rainfall matter more than the higher but less dependable yields of modern semi-dwarf durums. Sow into a firm seedbed in autumn following the first rains and avoid excess nitrogen, which encourages lodging in this comparatively tall-strawed heirloom type. Harvest only once heads have fully dried in the field.
sources: Institut National de la Recherche Agronomique de Tunisie (INRAT) — Tunisian durum wheat landrace collection
International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) — Durum wheat landraces of North Africa
